abstract: Biallelic variants in the voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) gene SCN1B are linked to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy type 52 (DEE52). SCN1B encodes two isoforms: transmembrane β1, generated by all 6 coding exons, and β1B, generated by exons 1 to 3 followed by retention of intron 3 ( SCN1B -IR). Transmembrane β1 subunits are multifunctional proteins that regulate sodium current and channel cell-surface expression, participate in cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesion, and modulate transcription. Several DEE52 variants in the transmembrane β1 coding region have been shown to result in mixed loss-of-function. DEE52 variants are also identified in SCN1B -IR, yet their functional impacts remain unknown. Here, we provide evidence that SCN1B -IR is a cell type–specific, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)–sensitive transcript. We investigate a severe biallelic DEE52 patient variant in intron 3, SCN1B c.449-2A>G, which results in expression of SCN1B -IR, but not transmembrane β1 transcripts. A transgenic mouse model that expresses SCN1B -IR, but not transmembrane β1, transcript phenocopies Scn1b null mice with seizures and early death. Thus, SCN1B -IR functions as an NMD-sensitive transcript that cannot compensate for the loss of transmembrane β1. We propose that future work may reveal SCN1B -IR to be a therapeutic target similar to other NMD-targeted transcripts.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: SCN1B intron 3 retention results in a nonsense-mediated decay–sensitive mRNA linked to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy

abstract: Biomolecular condensates selectively recruit and exclude proteins, and this partitioning is sometimes dictated by their intrinsically disordered regions. Factors that determine partitioning include client–scaffold interactions and stabilization of the scaffold network within the condensate, yet a molecular and predictive understanding has not been fully achieved. Here, we used coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate molecular interactions between two types of nuclear proteins as scaffolds: the charge-rich disordered region of Mediator 1 (MED1) and the aromatic-rich disordered region of Fused in Sarcoma (FUS), in mixtures with client intrinsically disordered regions from six different proteins. We show distinct partitioning into the MED1 and FUS condensates, while the presence of RNA in both dilute and dense phases modulated client partitioning. Favorable client–scaffold interaction energies within condensates were associated with client partitioning, while client–scaffold interactions competed with scaffold self-interactions. Analysis of interaction energies of individual residues revealed that the interactions were localized to specific sequence regions: charged blocks for interactions with MED1, and dispersed aromatic residues for interactions with FUS. Using residue–resolved interaction energies from our molecular dynamics simulations, we developed sequence-based predictors of client partitioning into MED1 and FUS condensates. Our prediction approach for partitioning can be extended to other biomolecules, offering a framework to analyze their partitioning in cellular environments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Molecular interactions underlying selective partitioning of clients into MED1 and FUS condensates

abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are important contributors to Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a key driver of oxidative inflammation released mainly by activated microglia in the neurodegenerative brain, is a potential therapeutic target to inhibit the neuroinflammatory cascade and oxidative damage in AD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, and achieving targeted brain delivery of an MPO inhibitor and minimizing systemic effects remain significant challenges. We addressed these limitations by first establishing that genetic deletion of MPO in the 5XFAD mouse model improved memory performance and reduced amyloid deposition, validating MPO as a therapeutic target. We then developed a liposome-encapsulated reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable MPO inhibitor (LERAMI). LERAMI uniquely combines targeted delivery with on-demand drug release, utilizing a ROS-sensitive linker to selectively release MPO inhibitors in ROS-rich regions within the AD microenvironment, minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In the 5XFAD mouse model. By reducing MPO expression and activity, LERAMI significantly improved cognitive performance, accompanied by decreased microglial activation, attenuated oxidative DNA damage, improved synaptic and neuronal density, and reduced amyloid burden. RNA sequencing revealed a robust hippocampal transcriptomic reprogramming, with upregulation of pathways critical for synaptic plasticity, calcium signaling, axon guidance, and neuroprotection, along with downregulation of inflammatory and immune response pathways. These findings demonstrate that targeted ROS-activatable MPO inhibition with LERAMI represents a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and potentially other neuroinflammatory diseases, offering a unique approach to mitigate neuroinflammation, preserve synaptic integrity, and restore cognitive function.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Intranasal delivery of a ROS-activatable myeloperoxidase inhibitor alleviates Alzheimer’s-like symptoms and pathology

abstract: Addressing climate change through mitigation and adaptation is expected to require more than $6 trillion in global investment annually by 2035. Yet many countries face significant barriers to accessing this finance, including low or absent credit ratings, large debt burdens, and high borrowing costs. Climate change may further amplify these barriers, creating a “vicious cycle” in which mounting economic losses reduce the capacity of countries to invest in adaptation and mitigation. We provide evidence that the cost and availability of capital for many countries have already been shaped by both historical exposure to naturally-occurring tropical cyclones (TCs) and anthropogenic warming. Our empirical estimates suggest that, on average across TC-exposed countries, 20% of debt-to-GDP ratios are attributable to TCs from 1980 to 2019. Across all countries, GDP levels are on average 12% lower due to the combined impacts of baseline naturally-occurring TCs and anthropogenic warming. In a separate correlational machine-learning analysis, we estimate that these macroeconomic impacts are associated with an increased likelihood of hotter countries receiving credit ratings below investment grade ( < BBB–), as well as persistent credit risk premiums of at least 1 basis point in 64 countries and 5 basis points in highly exposed countries. We provide estimates for 181 countries, including many TC-affected and/or hot countries that do not have bond yield data. Future increases in temperature and TC activity may further worsen sovereign credit conditions, potentially undermining climate resilience and long-run development prospects.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The debt burden of tropical cyclones and climate change

abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by gut microbiota are key modulators of intestinal homeostasis and immune responses. Although their anti-inflammatory roles are well established, the mechanisms by which SCFAs-FFAR2 shapes neutrophil function and influences intestinal inflammation remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate that dietary fiber or acetate protect mice from DSS-induced colitis despite increasing neutrophil infiltration into the intestinal tissue. Importantly, neutrophils are required for the protective effects of acetate, which are also dependent on FFAR2 signaling and IL-22. Neutrophil-specific deletion of FFAR2 impairs IL-22 responses, increases epithelial damage, and exacerbates colitis, while administration of recombinant IL-22 is sufficient to restore acetate protection in this context. Analysis of human ulcerative colitis biopsies reveals increased FFAR2 + neutrophils correlating with IL-22-related gene signatures. These findings indicate that acetate–FFAR2–neutrophil–IL-22 axis modulates intestinal inflammation, revealing a metabolic mechanism that links microbiota-derived signals to mucosal protection and highlighting potential therapeutic targets for inflammatory bowel diseases.
authors: Arilson Bernardo dos Santos Pereira Gomes
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Acetate–FFAR2 signaling induces neutrophil-derived IL-22 to protect against colitis

abstract: Endocytosis plays a crucial role in signaling, recycling, and degradation of receptors. Controlling endocytosis of specific receptors is therefore a major goal for both basic science and medicine. While antibody-induced dimerization can drive signaling-induced uptake of some receptors, the steric bulk of antibodies generally inhibits endocytosis, such that control over receptor uptake remains an unmet need. Recent work has demonstrated that attractive interactions between intrinsically disordered proteins drive inward membrane curvature, a key step in endocytosis. To harness this phenomenon for the control of receptor uptake, we designed chimeras that consisted of disordered domains fused to ligands for specific receptors. These chimeras condensed on membrane surfaces, in agreement with computational modeling, driving receptor clustering and uptake via clathrin-mediated endocytosis. In contrast, chimeras that repelled one another resisted condensation, helping receptors escape endocytosis and remain on the cell surface. Taken together, these results suggest that by modulating the amino acid sequence of intrinsically disordered ligands, we can promote or hinder the internalization of specific receptors by endocytic pathways. More broadly, these findings suggest a generalizable strategy for controlling the plasma membrane lifetime of diverse receptors, opening up new pathways for modulating cellular behavior and delivering therapeutics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Intrinsically disordered ligands for the control of receptor uptake by endocytosis

abstract: Evolution of genetic regulatory sequences is shaped by their genotype–phenotype map, but this map itself can evolve via changes in the molecular machinery that reads out the regulatory sequences. Using population genetics theory, we derive a maximization principle, which implies that genotype–phenotype maps will evolve to associate fit phenotypes with larger numbers of possible genotypes. Mathematically, this builds on analogies between population genetics and statistical physics, as well as optimal coding in information theory. The results are particularly interesting in the context of transcriptional regulation, where optimal values of certain parameters that determine the gene regulatory architecture can be derived even without a complete knowledge of the molecular mechanisms involved. We illustrate the theory using a simplified model of transcription factor (TF) binding to cis-regulatory elements (CREs): the fraction of possible CREs across the entire genotype space that bind a given TF evolves to match the fraction of CREs under selection to bind that TF. Similar “frequency matching” results are expected to emerge generically, because selection implicitly moves the entire regulatory architecture toward a fitness maximum, determining the “replicated genotype–phenotype map” for all CREs, while it simultaneously adapts toward individually fit CREs on that map. We discuss the subtleties and limitations of the theory related to biophysical constraints and the need for mutational robustness. Last, our theory suggests a possible mathematical definition for evolvability with predictive power that can be tested in evolutionary simulations and, ultimately, in comparative genetics studies.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Evolution, information content, and optimality of gene regulatory architectures

abstract: The transition to menopause is a period of profound physiological change that encompasses nearly one-third of a woman’s lifespan and is associated with a distinct rise in the incidence of psychosis. Despite the clinical burden of menopause-associated psychosis, the circuit-level mechanisms linking reproductive aging to psychiatric vulnerability remain poorly defined. Current understanding is limited by rodent models that utilize abrupt surgical hormone loss, which fail to capture the progressive endocrine fluctuations and follicular depletion characteristic of the natural menopausal transition. Here, we investigate how the gradual transition from perimenopause to postmenopause regulates the ventral hippocampus-mesolimbic dopamine circuit, a pathway centrally implicated in the development of psychotic symptoms. Specifically, we show that the perimenopausal transition induces a transient state of ventral hippocampal hyperactivity that selectively drives dopamine system dysfunction, whereas this modulatory control is absent in the postmenopausal state. These findings reveal that psychosis-related circuit instability is precipitated specifically by the hormonal transition itself, rather than the persistent state of estrogen deficiency that follows. This contrasts with the long-standing “estrogen protection hypothesis,” which posits that low hormone levels are the primary driver of symptoms and explains why standard hormone replacement and antipsychotic therapies often yield inconsistent results. Our results establish that perimenopause is a mechanistically distinct neurobiological window characterized by a unique failure of hippocampal-dopamine circuit regulation. By identifying this specific period of circuit instability, this work provides a framework for stage-specific psychiatric interventions and reframes reproductive aging as a series of distinct transitions in brain function.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A circuit mechanism for psychosis vulnerability during perimenopause

abstract: Voltage-gated sodium (Na v ) channels are targeted by animal peptide toxins, which serve as powerful molecular probes for dissecting channel structure-function relationships and lead molecules for drug discovery. β-scorpion toxins trap voltage sensor domains to remodel Na v channel gating, yet high-resolution structural evidence defining this process remains elusive. Here, we characterize LmNaTx1, a β-scorpion toxin from Lychas mucronatus . LmNaTx1 exerts state-dependent bimodal modulation on Na v 1.4: it facilitates channel activation while suppressing sodium conductance, accelerates slow-inactivation onset, and delays recovery from slow inactivation. We solved the 2.68 Å cryo-EM structure of the LmNaTx1-hNa v 1.4 complex, revealing that LmNaTx1 inserts into the extracellular cleft jointly formed by domain II voltage sensor (VSD II ) and the extracellular loop III (ECL III ) of the pore domain. Toxin binding remodels the S3–S4 II loop and displaces S0/S3 II helices to trap VSD II within a pre-activated intermediate state. MD simulations recapitulate step-wise VSD II conformational transitions and demonstrate that toxin-driven rearrangements tighten the intracellular pore gate. Mutagenesis combined with electrophysiology confirm that VSD II trapping remodels the activation and inactivation gating, whereas ECL III engagement contributes both to inhibition and activation. Subtype-specific sequence variations in the ECL III region underlie the prominent species- and isoform-dependent activities of the toxin toward insect and mammalian Na v channels. Our study provides a structural basis for the dual-action mechanisms of β-scorpion toxins on Na v channels and presents a structural framework for understanding toxin binding, channel gating modulation, ecological adaptation, and rational drug design.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Unconventional modulation of Na v 1.4 by a scorpion toxin through cooperative binding to voltage sensor and the pore domain

abstract: Specializations of blood vasculature in the central nervous system (CNS), including the blood–brain barrier (BBB), neurovascular coupling, and perivascular spaces, maintain CNS homeostasis and become dysfunctional in disease and aging. Protein turnover, the process by which proteins are continually degraded and replaced, profoundly influences cell and tissue function and is dysregulated in aging and disease. Understanding the turnover of neurovascular proteins could provide insight into how the vasculature achieves both long-term structural stability and dynamic regulation. Vascular proteins, however, are underrepresented in previous studies of in vivo brain protein turnover. In this work, we used stable isotope labeling, nonenzymatic blood vessel enrichment, and high-resolution mass spectrometry-based proteomics to quantify the half-lives of brain vascular proteins in young adult and aged mice. We report half-life estimates for 1,358 proteins, including components of endothelial junctions, BBB transporters, astrocyte endfoot proteins, and vascular basement membrane proteins. We found that certain classes of proteins with related functions had similar half-lives, including BBB junctional proteins (~3 d), BBB transporters (~2 to 6 d), and most basement membrane components (>30 d). We also identified peptide motifs enriched in proteins with short and long half-lives and found differences in half-life distributions for cell type–specific proteomes. Finally, although we did not observe a global age-related shift in vascular protein turnover, we did identify specific proteins with increased or decreased half-lives in aging. This work establishes a high-quality database of neurovascular protein half-lives and provides a foundation for understanding how protein turnover contributes to neurovascular function and age-associated dysfunction.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Neurovascular protein half-lives in health and aging

abstract: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role. In spite of this widespread pattern, the mechanisms behind the gender gap in persuasion are difficult to isolate and test in dynamic political conversations. Women may be less persuasive simply because role-based expectations prompt others to afford women less authority when speaking about politics generally or about some political topics. Alternatively, women may be less persuasive because they tend to use linguistic patterns or rhetorical strategies that are less effective. Using an original AI-based approach, we put 4,300 human subjects into realistic, real-time phone conversations with an AI agent. These agents were randomly assigned either a masculine or feminine gendered conversation topic and a male- or female-sounding voice, allowing us to manipulate topic and perceptions of speakers’ gender while holding constant other elements of rhetorical content and strategy. After validating the experimental treatments, we find no direct effects of perceived gender of the AI agent, as cued by voice. However, gender affects other important aspects of the persuasive interaction. Research subjects were more likely to be persuaded about the masculine topic (defense spending) than the feminine topic (aid to the poor). Additionally, women research subjects were, on average, more persuaded than men. To the extent that men and women emphasize different topics in political conversations and have different discussion partners, these dynamics are likely to shape women’s political persuasive influence.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The sound of persuasion: Using generative AI to identify gender gaps in political influence

abstract: Multiplexed protein imaging via DNA barcoding faces a fundamental scaling constraint: Each target requires a distinct DNA identity, making barcode capacity grow only linearly with the number of validated sequences. Combinatorial encoding in RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization achieves exponential scaling by distributing shared readout sequences across dozens of probes per transcript, but antibody-based protein labeling lacks this multiprobe architecture. Here, we report domain-encoded DNA barcodes (DEDBs), which embed combinatorial identity within the internal domain organization of a single-stranded DNA scaffold. Three orthogonal encoding units arranged across three encoding domains define a theoretical design space of 27 barcodes. Sequence reuse does not compromise readout specificity: Each read strand spans two adjacent domains, so a mismatched read strand inevitably contains a continuous stretch of noncomplementary bases and forms a thermodynamically disfavored intermediate that is subsequently displaced by the perfectly matched strand. We term this self-correcting behavior thermodynamic proofreading, and a three-process kinetic model shows that specificity arises not from initial binding discrimination but from cognate-driven correction at the product level. Coupled with signal-amplified antibody labeling, DEDBs enable quantitatively decoded nine-target intracellular protein imaging in fixed cells. The same barcode library supports Polychrome trajectory decoding for combinatorial identification and Monochrome cycle-resolved visualization for direct single-target inspection through reconfiguration of read-strand labeling. By generating combinatorial identities through the positional arrangement of reusable sequences within a single DNA strand, DEDBs reframe DNA barcode design from sequence enumeration to positional encoding.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Domain-encoded DNA barcodes for combinatorial multiplexed protein imaging via stepwise displacement

abstract: Mitochondrial function relies on the precise spatial coordination of protein synthesis and import. Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and must be supplied across varying intracellular distances. In highly polarized cells such as fungal hyphae and neurons, active long-distance mRNA transport is thought to sustain distal mitochondrial function, but its mechanistic coupling to protein import and organelle physiology is unclear. Here, we demonstrate that endosomal transport of mRNAs encoding mitochondrial proteins orchestrates local bioenergetics in infectious hyphae of Ustilago maydis . Using the subunit Atp3 of electron transport chain Complex V as a model, we uncover that the endosomal mRNA transporter Rrm4 is required for efficient mitochondrial protein import, particularly at growth poles. Loss of Rrm4 leads to defects in mitochondrial import, resulting in altered physiology. We propose that endosome-coupled mRNA transport constitutes a fundamental layer of subcellular mitochondrial homeostasis, with implications extending from fungal pathogenicity to neuronal disease.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Endosomal mRNA transport coordinates local mitochondrial bioenergetics during polar fungal growth

abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) comprise the major group of Ca 2+ -regulated kinases in plants and protists. These enzymes comprise an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal Ca 2+ -dependent activation domain (CAD). We solved the crystal structures of autoinhibited and activated forms of a plant CDPK, Arabidopsis CPK3. In the autoinhibited form, the CAD resembles a “dumbbell-like” calmodulin protein with a long helix in the N terminus that inhibits the kinase domain in a pseudo-substrate manner. Upon Ca 2+ binding to the four EF-hands, CAD undergoes a dramatic conformational change with a rotation around the kinase domain, thus exposing its active site for substrate recognition. Our structural and biochemical studies reveal that most plant CDPKs may involve distinct mechanisms of activation compared with CDPKs from the apicomplexan parasites.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Structural insights into inhibition and activation mechanisms of plant calcium-dependent protein kinases

abstract: Despite advances of biomimetic vesicles in cancer therapy, clinical challenges such as biosafety, scalability, and therapeutic efficacy remain significant hurdles. To address these limitations, we reveal the critical tumor-homing motifs of cancer cell membrane vesicles: a synergistic “chemotactic recruitment-adhesion anchoring” cascade effect, especially chemokine axes (e.g., CXCL12/CXCR4) and integrins (e.g., αVβ3). In this study, we identify autologous fibroblasts as an ideal “chassis” cell for engineering biomimetic carriers. Using this platform, we construct multigene-engineered fibroblast-derived nanovesicles (X-Fb-MNVs) coexpressing critical chemokine receptor CXCR4 and adhesion ligand iRGD, as well as PD-1 and CD47 protein, which achieved robust and broad-spectrum tumor targeting across breast, liver, pancreatic, and colon cancer PDX models. Significantly, CD47-modified X-Fb-MNVs reduced hepatic accumulation and phagocytic clearance, thereby minimizing off-target effects in vivo and improving tumor targeting efficiency. By loading diABZI STING agonist into X-Fb-MNVs with overexpressed PD-1, our system activates both T cell and innate immunity, reversing ICB resistance and achieving 83.3% survival with no tumor recurrence and long-term immune surveillance over 90 d, whereas no mice survived with free diABZI treatment. By merging multimodal targeting, immune reprogramming, and scalable production into a single platform, X-Fb-MNVs represent a remarkable biomimetic system with transformative potential for a wide-spectrum cancer immunotherapy.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multigene-engineered fibroblast-derived biomimetic vesicles for cancer multimodal targeting and immune reprogramming

abstract: Hormone pathways are central hubs in plant immunity, and their receptors, the critical initiators of signaling cascades, are logical targets of pathogen effectors. The jasmonic acid (JA) pathway is a cornerstone of defense against phytopathogens, especially necrotrophs. However, whether pathogens can directly target its receptor COI1 to subvert this defense layer has remained unclear. Here, we show that JA signaling positively regulates resistance to the devastating hemibiotrophic pathogen Ralstonia solanacearum and identified a bacterial effector, RipBO, that directly targets COI1 to counteract this defense. RipBO binds with high affinity to the F-box domain of COI1, competitively disrupts the COI1-ASK interaction, and thereby blocks SCF COI1 complex assembly. This disruption effectively stabilizes JAZ repressors and paralyzes JA-mediated immunity. Our findings clarify the contribution of JA signaling to bacterial wilt resistance and identify direct targeting of the hormone receptor as a pathogen virulence strategy, pointing to a potential vulnerability for crop protection.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Competitive disruption of COI1 receptor assembly by a hemibiotrophic bacterial effector suppresses jasmonate-mediated immunity

abstract: In living tissues, branched cells must efficiently cover territories to perform essential functions ranging from neural signaling to immune surveillance. However, how cells collectively establish and optimize tissue-scale coverage without global regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we develop a biophysical theory of interacting branched cells and show that coupling their growth to neighbor repulsion drives efficient tissue tiling with minimal territorial overlap. Strikingly, our model predicts that the same local mechanism progressively suppresses long-range density fluctuations during development, driving the system toward a large-scale order called hyperuniformity. We confirm these theoretical predictions on microglial patterning in the developing retina and show that in perturbation experiments with limited arbor growth, both tiling and fluctuation suppression are disrupted. Our results reveal that two seemingly distinct features of tissue organization, efficient space-filling and large-scale order, share a single dynamical origin, suggesting a general principle for robust tissue patterning.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Local interactions drive hyperuniform tissue coverage during development

abstract: Changes in fiber orientation in structurally anisotropic fibrous extracellular matrices govern transport, distribution, and accumulation of biologically active molecules and therapeutic nanoparticles in tissues. Fundamental studies of advection-driven transport in such matrices are challenging because changes in network anisotropy are generally coupled with variation in fiber dimensions, density, and surface chemistry. Here, a fibrous hydrogel was engineered in which the type and degree of fiber orientation were decoupled from these structural characteristics. Advection of charge-neutral nanoparticle probes under physiologically relevant pressure gradients was studied in a channel geometry that imposed spatially nonuniform flow across the fibrous network. The probe advection was quantified by the time of probe permeation through the gel along the fastest flow path and the time of probe distribution within the gel. We show that the permeation timescale was governed by advection along the pressure gradient, whereas the distribution timescale transitioned between advection- and diffusion-limited behavior depending on fiber orientation and probe dimension. The decoupling between these timescales became more pronounced with stronger alignment along the pressure gradient and with increasing probe dimension. Scaling analysis and a fluid dynamics simulation model further provided mechanistic insight into these experimental findings. Together, these results identify the key structural factors governing advection in anisotropic fibrous networks and provide a platform for future studies of the role of fiber orientation in tissues in regulating the transport, distribution, and dissemination of biologically active molecules, exosomes, and nanoparticle therapeutics under interstitial fluid flow.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Diffusive and advective transport in structurally anisotropic fibrous hydrogels

abstract: Rho-type GTPases of plants (ROPs) play essential roles in polarized cell growth, cell division, and organogenesis. Their activation depends on two types of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs): the plant-specific PRONE-domain-containing ROPGEFs and DOCK-type SPKGEFs. While ROPGEFs have been proposed to be autoinhibited in pollen and activated by receptor-like kinases (RLKs), the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using the moss Physcomitrium patens , we show that moss ROPGEF4 and ROPGEF6 exhibit low intrinsic GEF activity and are not autoinhibited by non-PRONE regions, whereas the catalytic domain of SPK1 and SPK6 is highly active. Through a candidate screen, we identified MLRK1, a malectin-like receptor kinase, as a ROPGEF-interacting protein. MLRK1 directly phosphorylates ROPGEF4 and ROPGEF6 and stimulates their GEF activities in vitro. These effects are attenuated by substituting key phosphosites (Ser231 in ROPGEF4 and Ser524/Thr526 in ROPGEF6) with nonphosphorylatable residues. Structural modeling, pull-down assays, and functional analyses indicate that phosphorylation enhances ROPGEF-ROP interactions and promotes the membrane localization of ROPGEF4/6. Furthermore, ROPGEFs are not essential for polarized cell growth on their own but act redundantly with SPK2. At the apical membrane, ROPGEFs appear to activate ROPs, reduce their diffusion, promote actin filament assembly and vesicle secretion, and ultimately facilitate cell expansion and growth. Collectively, our findings provide functional evidence that RLK-ROPGEF-ROP signaling module has emerged in early land plants and is involved in cell growth regulation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Activation of ROPGEFs by a malectin-like receptor kinase is involved in tip growth regulation in Physcomitrium patens

abstract: Cooper pairing in most of the known fermionic superfluids occurs via spin-1/2 quasiparticle interactions that lead to spin-singlet or spin-triplet pairing. In the topological semimetal YPtBi, strong spin–orbit coupling results in a band inversion between highly symmetric s - and p -like electronic bands and a degeneracy at the Γ point that ensures the manifold of j = 3/2 quasiparticle states thrive near the Fermi level, where superconducting pairing occurs. Here we study the effects of magnetic and nonmagnetic disorder and carrier density on this exotic superconducting pairing state. By varying levels of disorder and carrier densities by nearly two and three orders of magnitude, respectively, we show that the superconducting critical temperature of YPtBi has a remarkable robustness, with little variation across this span. Our results suggest that superconductivity in YPtBi may reside in a regime where phase stiffness, rather than pair formation, governs the transition temperature. The insensitivity of Cooper pairing to dramatic changes in quasiparticle environment in a j = 3/2 superconductor highlights a form of protection realized in topological high-spin superconductors.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Resilient j = 3/2 superconductivity in topological semimetal YPtBi

abstract: Glycosphingolipids are key components of the cell glycocalyx, yet the extent to which their anomeric configuration affects their membrane organization remains unclear. Glucosylceramide (GlcCer) exists as α- and β-anomers with distinct biological activities, while the biophysical basis for these differences is unknown. Here, using nitroxide spin-labeled analogs of α- and β-GlcCer, we examined how the glycosidic stereochemistry affects their partitioning in phospholipid bilayers. In 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-phosphatidylcholine, dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, and distearoylphosphatidylcholine liposomes, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra of both probes contained two components: a broad, motion-restricted component consistent with GlcCer incorporated into the lamellar lipid bilayer and a sharp, highly mobile component attributed to some segregated, bilayer-associated GlcCer-rich nano-assemblies. EPR spectral simulations and complementary analyses showed that α-GlcCer predominantly partitioned into the lamellar phospholipid phase, whereas β-GlcCer was strongly enriched in the segregated GlcCer-rich phase. Importantly, analogous anomer-dependent EPR behavior was also observed for aqueous GlcCer dispersions in the absence of phospholipids, indicating that the distinct assembly propensities are intrinsic to the glycolipids and are modulated, rather than created, by the phospholipids. These findings support a two-mesophase model in which anomeric configuration acts as a stereochemical switch that biases GlcCer between phospholipid lamellae and segregated glycolipid nano-assemblies. Notably, such anomer-dependent behaviors were observed at a probe loading of only 0.5 mol%. Thus, even at rather low abundance, a subtle stereochemical difference in GlcCer can substantially alter its compatibility with a phospholipid membrane matrix, providing a plausible physical basis for anomer-dependent glycolipid sorting, signaling, and disease-associated membrane organization.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Anomeric configuration encodes mesophase preference of glucosylceramides in phospholipid membranes

abstract: Single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) turned 30 this year. We argue that three advances usually treated as separate endeavors, i.e., high-information-content per-molecule readout, sequence-linked massive parallelism, and automated trajectory decoding, are in fact one convergence that is turning smFRET from a one-molecule-at-a-time measurement into a high-throughput conformational sequencer, a platform that measures dynamic conformational phenotypes across sequence space at scale. This perspective traces the 30-y arc, forecasts which advances will prove most transformative over the next decade, states the conditions on which that forecast depends, and identifies the bottlenecks that still remain.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Single-molecule FRET at 30: Toward conformational sequencing

abstract: Sensorimotor processing relies on high-frequency signaling across widespread neuronal networks, during which synapses undergo rapid short-term plasticity (STP) that transiently enhances or depresses synaptic strength. Although STP is known to vary across cell types and postsynaptic targets, it remains unclear whether and how it is regulated at the level of individual synaptic boutons along the same axon. Here, we used two-photon imaging of a fast genetically encoded glutamate sensor expressed in cerebellar granule cells to monitor glutamate release from individual parallel fiber boutons during trains of activity. We showed that along single axons, glutamate transients were detected at nearly all boutons, and displayed a high diversity of STP profiles. At individual boutons, initial synaptic weight and STP were regulated separately. Synaptic weight was primarily driven by release probability ( P r ) and the apparent number of functional release sites ( N ), whereas STP was mainly supported by rapid mobilization of synaptic vesicles. At the molecular level, we show that Synapsin II contributes to bouton-specific heterogeneity in release properties. These findings reveal that STP is regulated at the level of individual boutons by specific molecular determinants, enabling fine-tuned control of information flow in cerebellar circuits. A single granule cell could therefore translate an identical presynaptic spike pattern into distinct release dynamics at each of its boutons, thus diversifying the temporal structure of the information delivered to Purkinje cells.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Bouton-specific diversity of glutamate release from single parallel fiber axons in the cerebellum

abstract: Maintaining optimized nutrient exchange between partnered species across changing environments presents a fundamental challenge for nutritional mutualisms. Yet quantitative approaches linking nutrient acquisition by one partner with the nutritional requirements of the other have been lacking. Here we extend the Nutritional Geometry Framework from organisms and colonies to interspecific mutualisms by linking realized nutritional niches (RNNs) with nutritional performance landscapes to quantify nutritional homeostasis between interacting species. Nutritional analyses of thousands of DNA-barcoded plant fragments collected by free-ranging Panamanian leafcutter ants revealed that RNNs for fungal cultivar provisioning diverged between degraded urban and intact rainforest habitats. Despite this, colonies converged on similar nutritional intake targets that were similarly positioned relative to regions of high fungal performance, while fungal nutritional yield remained stable across habitats. These findings demonstrate that correspondence between colony nutritional intake and fungal nutritional performance provides a quantitative means of assessing nutritional homeostasis across interacting species and establishes a foundation for comparative analyses of nutrient exchange across mutualisms experiencing environmental change.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Nutritional niches reveal mutualism resilience in urban fungus-farming ants

abstract: The actin cytoskeleton is crucial to regulate cellular processes and morphology in eukaryotes, yet the tools to visualize it are not compatible with all organisms. In the apicomplexan Plasmodium falciparum , actin filaments are thought to be short and unstable, complicating their visualization. Here, we show that a tandem fusion of the actin-chromobody can label filaments in all P. falciparum red blood cell stages and observe actin structures in live cells with high spatiotemporal resolution. This work suggests that previous lack of labeling was due to suboptimal probes and that malaria blood stages have a filamentous and highly dynamic actin network.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Visualization of actin filaments in Plasmodium falciparum blood cell stages

abstract: Despite highly efficacious antiretroviral therapy (ART), durable ART-free remission remains a central objective of HIV-1 cure strategies. The randomized, placebo-controlled RIO trial recently demonstrated that long-acting broadly neutralizing anti-HIV-1 antibodies (bNAbs) can sustain prolonged virologic control after ART interruption, including control that persisted beyond the period of therapeutically relevant antibody concentrations, providing clinical evidence consistent with host-mediated suppression. However, the mechanisms underlying these “vaccinal” effects remain unresolved. Here, we establish Fcγ receptor (FcγR) engagement as an essential driver of multiyear remission after bNAb therapy in simian-human immunodeficiency virus (SHIV)-infected macaques. Brief therapy during acute infection with Fc domain variants of the bNAb 3BNC117, matched for antigen binding, neutralizing activity, and pharmacokinetics but differing in FcγR engagement, produced comparable early virologic control yet profoundly divergent long-term outcomes. Sustained CD8 T cell–dependent suppression lasting nearly 300 wk developed in every evaluable animal receiving the FcγR-engaging variant but arose in only one of eight recipients of the FcγR-null variant. FcγR-driven immunomodulation imprinted a CD8 T cell response characterized by enhanced antigen-specific effector function, early clonal focusing with sustained clonotype persistence, and distinct cellular-state transcriptional signatures. Our findings identify the Fc–FcγR axis as a critical determinant of the reliable induction of durable remission and provide a mechanistic framework for developing Fc-engineered bNAbs designed to enhance vaccinal immunity and advance antibody-based strategies with the potential to achieve functional cure.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Durable CD8-mediated remission after brief anti-HIV-1 antibody treatment requires FcγR engagement

abstract: We establish a remarkably rich ground state phase diagram in the maple-leaf lattice spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet as a function of the three symmetry-inequivalent nearest-neighbor bonds using exact diagonalization and tower-of-states analysis on clusters up to $N=36$ sites. Besides a hexagonal plaquette state, a star-shaped valence bond solid state is discovered in close vicinity to the (canted) $120^\circ$ magnetic phase, strongly reminiscent of a de-confined critical point or Dirac spin liquid scenario on the triangular lattice antiferromagnets. Moreover, an exact dimer product-state is observed next to a collinear Néel-state, similar to the Shastry-Sutherland model. All identified phases compete in a parameter regime close to the isotropic point, providing a promising region for spin liquids to emerge. By analyzing Gutzwiller-projected wave-functions we identify a sliver of parameter regime where a gapped $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ spin liquid Ansatz is in astonishing agreement with the exact $N=36$ ground state. This rich competition of paramagnetic phases demonstrates that the maple-leaf antiferromagnet is a promising platform for exotic states of matter and quantum critical phenomena.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Competing paramagnetic phases in the maple-leaf Heisenberg antiferromagnet

abstract: We study correlation functions in conserved nonequilibrium mixtures, including multi-temperature systems and non-reciprocal field theories. The corresponding linear theory is short-ranged, and nonlinearities are irrelevant in the renormalization-group sense. Nonetheless, we find that these nonlinearities generate long-ranged three-point correlations in the isotropic disordered phase. Our analytical predictions, which are based on a phenomenological theory, are confirmed by numerical simulations of Brownian colloids in contact with thermal baths at different temperatures. Dangerously irrelevant nonlinearities in nonequilibrium mixtures thus offer a new route to long-range correlations, supporting the hypothesis that such correlations are not the exception but the rule out of equilibrium.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Generic long-range correlations in conserved nonequilibrium mixtures

abstract: We prove that the entanglement of formation of every two-mode Gaussian state coincides with its Gaussian restriction, solving a longstanding open problem in continuous variable quantum information theory. The key result is a sharp affine relation between entanglement and a generalized Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen observable, valid for arbitrary pure two-mode states, including non-Gaussian ones. We further prove that the entanglement of formation is additive on arbitrary tensor products of two-mode Gaussian states, and hence coincides with the entanglement cost, settling the latter for all two-mode Gaussian states. As a consequence, we obtain in closed form the entanglement cost of thermal-loss, thermal-amplifier and additive-noise bosonic channels. Our results, which also extend to bisymmetric multimode states, establish that no two-mode state is less entangled than the Gaussian state with the same covariance matrix, yielding measurable lower bounds on both the entanglement of formation and the entanglement cost of arbitrary non-Gaussian states.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Optimality of Gaussian entanglement of formation

abstract: The presence of low-energy valley excitations in Si/SiGe heterostructures often causes spin qubits to fail. It is therefore important to develop robust protocols for characterizing the valley coupling. Here, we show that realistically sized samplings of valley energy distributions tend to dramatically overestimate the average valley coupling. But we find that knowledge of the valley phase, in addition to the valley splitting, can significantly improve our estimates. Motivated by this understanding, we propose a novel method to probe the valley phase landscape across the quantum well using simple g-factor measurements. An important calibration step in this procedure is to measure g in a loop enclosing a valley vortex, where the valley phase winds by 2 π around a zero of the valley splitting. This proposal establishes an important new tool for probing spin qubits, and it can be implemented in current experiments.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Statistical characterization of valley coupling in Si/SiGe quantum dots via g -factor measurements near a valley vortex

abstract: Understanding lattice vibrations in two-dimensional (2D) materials is essential for controlling thermal transport, mechanical response, and energy dissipation in nanoscale devices. However, the intrinsic lifetimes of low-energy phonon modes, particularly those that are optically silent, remain largely unexplored. Here we use helium-3 spin-echo spectroscopy to resolve low-energy phonons at the surface of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and measure their intrinsic linewidths. We report the simultaneous observation of multiple surface-confined interlayer shear modes whose energies agree closely with linear-chain model predictions. By resolving their intrinsic linewidths, we demonstrate a strong confinement-dependent reduction in phonon lifetimes, with a near order-of-magnitude increase in linewidth between the four- and two-layer modes, substantially exceeding simple inverse-layer-number scaling. The three- and four-layer linewidths show no statistically resolved temperature dependence over the measurement range, consistent with a substantial temperature-independent contribution. We also observe the flexural and Rayleigh wave modes and extract the bending rigidity of a quasi-freestanding hBN monolayer. The systematic broadening with decreasing effective layer number suggests that confinement strongly influences phonon decay. These results reveal how reduced dimensionality affects the decay of interlayer shearing modes in hBN, providing direct insight into the phonon lifetimes, confinement effects, and dissipation pathways that govern the dynamical behaviour of two-dimensional materials.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Intrinsic linewidths of confined phonons in few-layer hBN

abstract: We report a measurement of the charged-current coherent pion production cross section on argon using the MicroBooNE liquid argon time projection chamber exposed to the Booster Neutrino Beam at Fermilab. The measurement uses the MicroBooNE data set corresponding to 1.26 × 10 21 protons on target with a mean neutrino energy of 0.8 ~GeV. The flux-averaged cross section is measured to be ( 9.1 ± 1.2 stat ± 1.2 syst ) × 10 − 40 cm 2 / Ar . This result represents the first measurement of charged-current coherent pion production on argon at sub-GeV neutrino energies. Due to its clean two-body kinematics, where the neutrino interacts coherently with the entire nucleus producing a forward muon and pion with no nuclear breakup, this process provides a useful tool for constraining neutrino flux uncertainties in current and future oscillation experiments such as DUNE.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: First measurement of sub-GeV ν μ charged-current coherent pion production on argon in MicroBooNE

abstract: Higher-spin symmetry is known to mix lower-spin fields with higher-spin fields, creating a complex interaction picture where no closed finite field sector is expected to exist for dimensions greater than three. By studying the self-dual part of higher-spin interaction vertices in four dimensions, we show that gauge fields of spins greater than two can be consistently set to zero. In this case, the fields with helicities $-2\leqλ\leq 0$ form a closed sub-sector and also act as sources for positive helicities. For these lower spin fields, we identify their equations of motion. In particular, we show that self-dual gravity with a cosmological constant emerges as a unique rigid part of higher-spin interactions. Notably, its equations have a form that incorporates the Moyal star product, which is essential for generating the higher-spin algebra. Therefore, we demonstrate that self-dual gravity can be derived from higher-spin symmetries.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Self-dual gravity from higher-spin theory

abstract: Surface roughness can either increase or decrease friction depending on the dominant mechanism: smoothing reduces friction by suppressing asperity-induced deformation, but can increase friction by enhancing interfacial adhesion. Here, we show that, for dry glass–glass contacts, increasing nanoscale roughness can reduce friction because it suppresses triboelectric adhesion. As the root-mean-square surface slope h’rms of the glass ball is increased from 0.01 to 0.09, the friction coefficient drops by about 30%, despite a threefold increase in the average contact pressure. Using rheometer-based friction measurements in dry nitrogen, super-resolution imaging of the real contact area, soft X-ray discharge, and Faraday-cup electrometry, we show that increasing roughness reduces both the real contact area and retained tribocharge, thereby weakening the electrostatic contribution to friction. Discharging the interface with soft X-rays largely removes the roughness dependence of friction. Our results establish tribocharging as an adhesion mechanism through which nanoscale roughness controls friction in dry dielectric contacts.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Roughness-controlled tribocharging governs friction in dry glass contacts

abstract: A key property of a global symmetry's anomaly is its order: the smallest integer $n$ for which the diagonal symmetry of the $n$-copy system is anomaly-free. While many familiar lattice anomalies have finite order, perturbative anomalies in the continuum$-$those captured by Feynman diagrams$-$have infinite order. In this paper, we show that the Onsager symmetry, a lattice realization of the chiral symmetry of a 1+1d massless Dirac fermion, has an order-two anomaly. However, imposing lattice CPT symmetry enhances this anomaly from order two to infinite order, yielding a lattice chiral symmetry structure that more faithfully matches the continuum chiral anomaly. We also discuss the corresponding 2+1d symmetry-protected topological phases for these infinite-order lattice anomalies.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Infinite-order lattice chiral anomalies and C P T symmetry

abstract: Spin supersolids emerge as a central topic in frustrated magnetism, motivating the search for realization in quantum materials. To this end, we study the origin of exchange anisotropy, Δ , in triangular-lattice cobaltate families X 2 Y Co(PO 4 ) 2 and X 2 Co(SeO 3 ) 2 ( X = Na, K, Rb, Cs; Y = Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) by tailoring realistic spin models. We show that Δ is determined by the ratio of trigonal splitting to spin–orbit coupling strength. This framework explains contrasting anisotropies in these families, predicts systematic trends in Δ across X / Y -substitutions, and identifies candidate materials for spin supersolids. Our results establish trigonal splitting engineering as a microscopic route toward the design of spin supersolids.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Microscopic design rule for spin supersolids in triangular-lattice magnets

abstract: Quantum spin liquids with long-range entanglement are of great interest for applications in quantum technology. The quantum spin ice Pr$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ is a promising example, where it is believed that structural disorder plays a key role in enhancing quantum mechanical effects by introducing strains that split the ground state doublet akin to the effect of a local disordered transverse field. However, the precise defect structure responsible for this behaviour is unknown. Here we have determined the intrinsic defect structure of Pr$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ using neutron and x-ray scattering techniques supported by density functional theory. We find the main defect is the stuffing of Zr$^{4+}$ sites by Pr$^{3+}$ ions, accompanied by charge compensating O$^{2-}$ vacancies, and the relaxation of a neighbouring O$^{2-}$ ion to an interstitial site. Our results explain the single-ion magnetism by considering the non-magnetic singlets that arise on neighbouring sites as a result of the defect structure. These singlets account for additional features in the crystal electric field excitations. The effects caused by this low level of structural disorder are magnified since several neighbouring Pr sites are affected. This makes a significant contribution towards the observed broadening of pinch points in the magnetic diffuse scattering, which was previously attributed purely to quantum effects.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Intrinsic disorder in the candidate quantum spin ice Pr 2 Zr 2 O 7

abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation is one of the core subroutines in quantum algorithms. This paper gives a parallelized amplitude estimation (PAE) algorithm that simultaneously achieves near-Heisenberg scaling in the total number of queries and sub-linear scaling in the circuit depth, with respect to the estimation precision. The algorithm is composed of a global GHZ state followed by separated low-depth Grover circuits optimized by quantum signal processing techniques; the number of qubits in the GHZ state and the depth of each circuit is tunable as a trade-off way, which particularly enables even near-Heisenberg-limited and logarithmic-depth algorithm for amplitude estimation. We prove that this trade-off scaling is nearly optimal with use of the parallel quantum adversary method, against folklore on the impossibility of efficient parallelization in amplitude estimation. The proposed algorithm has a form of distributed quantum computing, which may be suitable for device implementation.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Near-Heisenberg-limited parallel amplitude estimation with logarithmic-depth circuits

abstract: Non-Abelian anyons emerging in fractional quantum Hall states carry a characteristic entropy, $ΔS = k_B \log d$, where $d$ is the anyon's quantum dimension. This $\mathcal{O}(1)$ entropy can, in principle, be extracted from charge measurements of an antidot via Maxwell relations. However, equilibrium charge measurements in fractional antidots have proven to be challenging with conventional charge detectors. Here, we propose a scheme based on an antidot embedded in an interferometer, in which the charge can be inferred from the recently observed time-dependent switching of the interference phase. Performing such non-local charge measurements at equilibrium, the characteristic $\mathcal{O}(1)$ entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., $d = \sqrt{2}$ for the $ν= 5/2$ state) can be extracted for intermediate temperatures, which exceed the level spacing of the interferometer edge, but are much smaller than the level spacing of the antidot.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Entropy of non-Abelian anyons from slow quasiparticle dynamics in quantum Hall interferometers

abstract: Understanding defect physics under operational conditions is essential for advancing perovskite photovoltaics, as traditional dark-state characterization fails to capture critical electronic processes, such as the interactions between defects and excited carriers, that govern real device performance. Here we directly probe the electronic response of Schottky defects in CH₃NH₃PbBr₃ to illumination using in-operando laser-illuminated cross-sectional scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy. High-resolution spectroscopic mapping, combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations, reveals a localized shift in the valence band near defects, without the emergence of in-gap states or changes of the conduction band. The resulting band-edge modulation, inaccessible to dark measurements, promotes local electron–hole separation while suppressing trap-assisted recombination, establishing a microscopic mechanism for photo-enhanced defect tolerance.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Atomically resolved photoenhanced defect tolerance in metal-organic hybrid perovskites

abstract: We report on the first experimental verification of mode-independent entanglement. Commonly, the entanglement of a state is firmly based on pre-defined parties that are correlated, and the state might be disentangled when the definition of the parties is changed. Exceeding this party-dependent concept, we realize a type of quantum entanglement that persists even if the parties, in our case modes, are transformed. This safeguards the performance of entanglement in real-world applications, such as quantum communication settings involving noise and untrusted parties. For the state generation, we present an experimental scheme based on a fully reconfigurable temporally multiplexed interferometer with measurement-induced nonlinearities, which generates heralded two-photon states in two modes that are entangled for all choices of orthonormal mode basis. For the certification process, we utilize a tailored quantum-state tomography, achieving fidelities that validate the presence of mode-independent entanglement as a resilient and operationally advantageous quantum correlation.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Demonstration of unpartible entanglement

abstract: Large-momentum-transfer techniques are instrumental for the next generation of atom interferometers as they significantly improve their sensitivity. State-of-the-art implementations rely on elastic scattering processes from optical lattices such as Bloch oscillations or sequential Bragg diffraction, but their performance is constrained by imperfect pulse efficiencies. Here we develop a Floquet-based theoretical framework that provides a unified description of elastic light–atom scattering across all relevant regimes. This formalism enables an efficient exploration of the parameter space, including quasi-momentum preparation, and reveals previously unexplored operating regimes in which tailored Floquet states exhibit orders-of-magnitude reduced losses. In addition, phase extrema of excited Floquet states provide enhanced robustness against lattice-parameter fluctuations. The model is validated through direct comparison with numerical solutions of the Schrödinger equation and through quantitative agreement with recent experimental benchmark results. Our findings establish new, practical operating regimes for large-momentum-transfer beam splitters and open promising perspectives for precision atom interferometry in fundamental physics, gravity gradiometry, and gravitational-wave detection.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Fundamental limits of large momentum transfer in optical lattices

abstract: We establish an exact theory of coherence spectrum transformation in nonunitary wave scattering. For any linear system and input coherence, we prove the attainable output spectra are fully determined by a determinant equality and Horn’s inequalities—necessary and sufficient conditions from matrix theory applied to coherence physics for the first time. Every allowed spectrum is physically realizable via unitary control of the input; we solve this inverse problem constructively via manifold optimization. The results apply to any linear system regardless of geometry or scattering strength.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Coherence spectrum transformation in nonunitary wave scattering

abstract: The emergence of heavy quasiparticles in a Kondo lattice is usually viewed as the formation of a low-energy hybridization gap. Whether this gap represents a rigid electronic structure or a fragile many-body state that can be dynamically reconfigured remains a central question for heavy-fermion systems near magnetic order, quantum criticality, and unconventional superconductivity. Here we use femtosecond pump-probe reflectivity to interrogate this problem in the weakly hybridized Kondo-lattice compound CePt$_2$In$_7$. At low fluence, a slow quasiparticle relaxation channel emerges below $T^* \sim$ 40 K and follows a Rothwarf-Taylor bottleneck response with a low-energy recombination scale 2$Δ\approx$ 7.4 meV. Coherent optical phonons, independently identified by Raman spectroscopy, act as an internal lattice thermometer and rule out large quasi-equilibrium lattice heating as the origin of the nonlinear electronic response. The phonon-free electronic amplitude $A_{\rm elec}$ reveals a fluence-reversal fingerprint: with cooling from the hybridization-crossover regime, the response evolves from weak-linear behavior to Rothwarf-Taylor-like bottleneck suppression and finally to anomalous high-fluence enhancement at the lowest temperatures. This reversal cannot be accounted for by a rigid fixed-gap bottleneck alone and instead identifies an ultrafast optical signature of photoinduced redistribution of a fragile Kondo-hybridized electronic response.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Ultrafast fluence-reversal fingerprint of nonequilibrium Kondo-hybridized response in CePt 2 In 7

abstract: Inertialess elastic instabilities can profoundly affect transport in complex-fluid flows, from mixing in microfluidic devices and displacement through porous media to polymer processing. While such instabilities are well understood in flows with curved streamlines, their origin in rectilinear flows like the prototypical Kolmogorov flow remains unresolved. Here, we report the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability, at vanishing inertia, in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, driven by electromagnetic forcing. The instability is characterized by the emergence of "arrow-shaped" structures in the velocity field, which fluctuates chaotically as the forcing strength increases. We reproduce these observations in simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and trace the dynamics in the confined flow to the travelling arrowhead structures that emerge from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow. Our work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows, broadening the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Experimental evidence of elastic instability in viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow

abstract: The scalability of physical qubit numbers is a central challenge toward a universal fault-tolerant quantum computer. Here, we robustly trap 11,000 individual atoms in a tweezer array, thereby enabling the available single atom resource above the 10,000-atom level for the first time in neutral atom quantum computation platforms. This advance is enabled by a single metasurface, approximately 2 cm in diameter, that generates the entire tweezer array without the need for microscope objectives, thereby maximizing laser-power efficiency. The large aperture ensures a working distance of about 1.5 cm, allowing the metasurface to be placed outside the vacuum cell and avoiding the technical complications of in-vacuum operation. We further characterize the randomly loaded atom array using the statistical theory of percolation phase transitions. This work takes an important first step toward a quantum computer at the 10,000-qubit scale.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Trapping 11 thousand atoms in a tweezer array generated by a single metasurface
